newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. says APEC stand on info pact "significant".
newsitem.headline: U.S. says APEC stand on info pact "significant".

text.p: The United States said on Saturday Asia-Pacific nations had taken a significant stand by endorsing efforts to conclude a global agreement on free trade in computers and telecommunications equipment.

Trade and foreign ministers at the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference agreed to endorse the U.S.-led effort to conclude an Information Technology Agreement by next month's inaugural meeting of the World Trade Organisation in Singapore.
But it was far from the ringing endorsement Washington had sought, delegates said.

"Ministers endorsed the efforts at WTO to conclude an information technology agreement by the Singapore Ministerial Conference and urged all other members of the WTO to work toward that end," the APEC ministers said in a statement.

Delegates at the conference described the wording as a watered-down version of what the United States had originally wanted -- APEC's endorsement for zero tariffs on information technology trade by 2000.
The stakes are high. The United States says the business is worth at least $1 trillion a year, 80 percent of that in the booming Asia-Pacific region.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Washington had never expected such an endorsement from APEC.

"What the U.S. had sought from APEC was the political will to conclude an agreement in Singapore...and that was what was achieved," she told a news conference after the two-day ministerial conference.
"This is a significant agreement because it is the first time APEC has taken a stand on a WTO issue," she said. APEC, grouping 18 economies on the Pacific Rim, was founded in 1989.
Repeatedly questioned over the issue, Barshefsky said Washington never intended to negotiate the ITA at APEC.
The pact was being negotiated at the WTO in Geneva "where the experts are". And besides, the European Union, a key player in agreeing such a pact, is not an APEC member, she said.
Malaysia led opposition to the pact.

"First of all we did not reach agreement at APEC on information technology and negotiations for that technology," Malaysian Minister of Trade and Industry Rafidah Aziz said at a joint news conference with the other ministers.
She had said earlier that Malaysia wanted flexibility on the timeframe for achieving free trade in information technology and the kinds of products covered.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, who arrived on Saturday for Monday's summit, told a news conference: "We can support it (ITA) to the extent that it doesn't hurt us."
Hong Kong Secretary of Trade and Industry Denise Yue told reporters U.S. delegates said there could be flexibility as to the timetable and products covered in the pact.
That would represent a significant softening of the U.S. stand, delegates said.

At the news conference, Barshefsky said the Geneva talks on an ITA "were predicated on zero tariffs by 2000, recognising that some countries will have specific exceptions" to the products that are covered.
